headline: MoE vs Dense: Local AI Model Showdown
summary: Hugging Face breaks down the architectural trade-offs between Mixture-of-Experts and dense models for local inference. Understand routing mechanics, memory patterns, and deployment realities to pick the right architecture for your hardware.

slides.title: MoE vs Dense: Which Local Model Wins?
slides.subtitle: Architecture showdown for on-device AI inference
slides.body: Hugging Face publishes deep technical comparison of Mixture-of-Experts versus dense transformer architectures. The verdict reshapes how engineers choose models for local deployment.
slides.deep_dive: As local AI inference explodes, the architecture choice becomes critical. Dense models activate all parameters for every token. MoE models route tokens to specialized expert subnetworks, activating only a fraction of total parameters. This fundamental difference cascades into memory bandwidth, latency, and hardware utilization patterns that determine real-world performance on consumer GPUs.
slides.key_fact: MoE activates subset of parameters per token; dense activates all parameters every forward pass.
slides.why_it_matters: Wrong architecture choice wastes VRAM, kills latency, or exceeds hardware limits.

slides.title: Architecture Shift: Sparse Activation Enters Local Inference
slides.subtitle: MoE brings conditional computation to consumer hardware
slides.body: Traditional dense transformers use fixed computation. MoE introduces dynamic routing — only relevant experts process each token. This sparsity changes memory access patterns and compute utilization fundamentally.
after_items: Subset of experts active per token
slides.deep_dive: The shift mirrors CPU branch prediction: instead of executing all instructions, the model predicts which expert subnetworks are relevant. Router networks learn to specialize experts — some handle syntax, others reasoning, others domain knowledge. This specialization emerges during training without explicit labels.
slides.key_fact: MoE replaces fixed computation with learned routing decisions per token.
slides.why_it_matters: Enables larger effective model capacity within same active parameter budget.

slides.title: Inside MoE: Router, Experts, and Load Balancing
slides.subtitle: Token-level routing replaces monolithic feed-forward layers
slides.body: Each MoE layer replaces a dense FFN with multiple expert FFNs. A router network computes affinity scores, top-k experts process the token, outputs are weighted and combined.
slides.deep_dive: The router is a tiny linear layer projecting token hidden states to expert logits. Softmax produces probabilities. Top-k gating (typically k=1 or 2) selects experts. Crucially, load balancing losses prevent router collapse — where all tokens route to same experts. Auxiliary losses encourage uniform expert utilization. During inference, only selected experts' weights are loaded from VRAM, creating irregular memory access.
slides.key_fact: Router learns specialization without supervision; load balancing prevents expert collapse.
slides.why_it_matters: Sparse activation enables 10x+ parameter count with same active compute.

slides.title: Conceptual Performance Profile (Source: Qualitative Analysis)
slides.subtitle: No synthetic numbers — understand the trade-off vectors
slides.body: Source provides qualitative comparison. Key dimensions: throughput, latency variance, VRAM efficiency, and quality per active parameter.

metrics.label: Throughput (tokens/sec)
metrics.value: MoE higher at same active params

slides.deep_dive: The article emphasizes that benchmarks depend heavily on hardware, batch size, and sequence length. MoE shines when total parameters exceed VRAM — inactive experts can stay in system RAM or disk. Dense models win when everything fits in VRAM and batch sizes are large enough to saturate compute. Latency variance in MoE comes from expert load imbalance and dynamic memory access.
slides.key_fact: MoE advantages emerge at scale; dense wins in VRAM-fit regimes.
slides.why_it_matters: Match architecture to your hardware constraint, not just model size.

slides.title: Local Inference Constraints: Before and After MoE Adoption
slides.subtitle: MoE unlocks model sizes previously impossible on consumer GPUs
slides.body: Dense models forced hard choices: quantize aggressively, offload to CPU, or accept tiny context. MoE changes the constraint surface.
before_items: Context length limited by KV cache
slides.deep_dive: The paradigm shift: total parameter count no longer equals active compute. A 70B MoE with 8 experts per layer and top-2 routing activates ~17B parameters per token — comparable to a 13B dense model — but with 70B total capacity for knowledge storage. Inactive experts (53B params) sit in system memory, loaded on-demand. This is virtual memory for model weights.
slides.key_fact: MoE decouples model capacity from active compute budget.
slides.why_it_matters: Run GPT-3-scale models locally without quantization compromise.

slides.title: Deployment Patterns: When Teams Choose Each Architecture
slides.subtitle: Real engineering decisions based on hardware and latency SLAs
slides.body: Engineering teams select architecture based on deployment target, not just benchmark leaderboards.
slides.deep_dive: Edge deployment (phones, laptops): Dense models dominate. Predictable memory, no routing overhead, mature quantization tooling (GGUF, AWQ). Server-side batch inference: MoE wins. Large batch sizes amortize routing cost, expert parallelism across GPUs, higher throughput per dollar. Hybrid serving: Dense for low-latency tier, MoE for high-quality tier. Some teams cascade — route easy queries to dense, hard queries to MoE.
slides.key_fact: Architecture choice maps to deployment tier: edge=dense, server=MoE, hybrid=cascade.
slides.why_it_matters: Wrong choice costs 10x inference spend or violates latency SLA.

slides.title: Evaluate, Adapt, Optimize: Your MoE Adoption Path
slides.subtitle: Step-by-step validation before committing to architecture
slides.body: Follow this sequence to avoid costly architecture mismatches.
items: Profile VRAM budget vs model size requirements
Benchmark dense baseline on target hardware
Test MoE variant with same active param count
Load test with production traffic patterns
slides.deep_dive: Critical insight: MoE quantization is less mature. Expert-specific quantization sensitivity varies — some experts tolerate 4-bit, others need 8-bit. Router weights are extremely sensitive. Test per-expert quantization. Also verify your inference engine supports expert parallelism and dynamic loading. Many engines still treat MoE as dense with masking, losing memory benefits.
slides.key_fact: MoE quantization and engine support lag dense; validate before commit.
slides.why_it_matters: Skipping validation risks silent quality degradation or OOM crashes.

slides.title: Match Architecture to Constraint, Not Hype
slides.subtitle: MoE and dense each own a regime — know yours
slides.body: Hugging Face analysis confirms: no universal winner. Dense for edge, predictability, maturity. MoE for server-scale, capacity-per-VRAM, quality-per-active-param. Your hardware dictates the choice.
takeaways: Dense models: default for edge, low-latency, mature tooling
MoE models: default for server batch, VRAM-constrained quality
Profile active params, not total params, for compute budgeting
